newsitem.title: GERMANY: German watchdog starts Vulkan insider probe.
newsitem.headline: German watchdog starts Vulkan insider probe.

text.p: Germany's securities trading watchdog, the BAWe, on Tuesday said it had begun initial investigations into suspicions of alleged insider trading in shares of the now bankrupt shipbuilder Bremer Vulkan AG.
But the BAWe, the Federal Supervisory Authority for Securities Trading, downplayed a press report naming an official said to be under investigation.
"We cannot rule anything out at this stage. But the probe has only just begun," said BAWe spokesman Juergen Oberfrank. "It is far too premature to name names."

The city state of Bremen, where the defunct company is headquartered, had been a major guarantor of loans made to Vulkan to finance shipbuilding and has been taking a leading role in attempts to find a solution to the group's woes.

Oberfrank said the investigation related to a period prior to April 28, when several German newspapers reported that two large companies, later named as utility Veba AG and steelmaker Thyssen AG, were interested in buying Vulkan.
Both companies denied that report, which prompted fresh interest in Vulkan's stock, still traded because the firm remains officially registered.

Vulkan shares more than trebled in value in late April, surging from 2.60 marks on April 23 to 9.90 marks on April 28. The shares, which have a nominal value of 50 marks, traded at 5.80 marks on Tuesday.
The BAWe was currently examining records of trades in Bremer Vulkan in late April and had not yet decided whether to proceed to a second stage, Oberfrank said.

That would involve contacting Bremer Vulkan or other connected individuals directly, he said, conceding that the agency's job would likely be complicated by the fact that the shipping company in effect no longer exists as a conventional firm, having collapsed spectacularly in May 1996.
No comment was immediately available from Vulkan's receiver, Jobst Wellensiek.
The BAWe has been steadily upping its activities to curb insider trading, which was outlawed in Germany for the first time in 1994.
The agency began 329 routine insider trading probes in the first quarter of 1997 and had carried 22 to a further stage.
A total of 11 cases, where there were concrete suspicions of insider trading, had been passed to public prosecutors in that time.
The BAWe's most spectacular case to date centres on software maker SAP AG after the agency earlier this month passed on evidence of alleged insider trading in its shares to Frankfurt prosecutors.
That investigation is still continuing with a ruling not expected for several months.
